planting.note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in summer or plant container specimens in spring in well-drained, average soil; Tom Thumb is an extremely slow-growing dwarf selection that needs a decade or more to reach its small mature size, so start with a good-sized container plant.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in partial shade to full sun, providing a bit of shelter from harsh afternoon exposure in hot climates. Tom Thumb is a dwarf, dense, naturally rounded selection of kohuhu whose small, wavy-edged leaves emerge bronze-green and darken to a deep purple-black through the season, giving the whole shrub a rich, almost inky foliage color that intensifies with more sun. Growth is very slow, so this cultivar keeps a tidy, ball-shaped form with minimal pruning for many years, making it useful for low hedging, foundation planting, or as a dark-foliage accent among lighter-colored perennials. It shares the fine-textured, wind- and salt-tolerant constitution of the species and tolerates being clipped if a more formal shape is wanted.

common_name: Garnettii Pittosporum (Variegated Grey-Green Kohuhu with Pink-Tinged Winter Margins)

planting.note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in summer or plant container specimens in spring in well-drained, average soil in partial shade to full sun; Garnettii forms an upright, columnar shrub useful for screening and mixed hedges without heavy pruning.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in partial shade to full sun, sheltered from the coldest winter winds at the northern edge of its range. Garnettii is a vigorous, upright selection of kohuhu with grey-green leaves broadly edged in creamy white, and the white margins flush an attractive soft pink in cold weather, adding seasonal interest that most variegated shrubs lack. Its columnar-to-conical habit makes it a favorite for informal screens, mixed borders, and clipped hedging in mild-winter gardens, and the pale, honey-scented spring flowers are inconspicuous but pleasant near a path or patio. It tolerates coastal wind and salt spray well and responds to shearing if a denser, more formal shape is desired.

planting.note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in summer or plant container-grown specimens in spring in well-drained, average to poor soil in partial shade to full sun; Karo is exceptionally tolerant of wind, salt spray, and coastal exposure, making it a top choice for seaside screening.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average to poor soil in partial shade to full sun; Karo is a robust New Zealand coastal native that grows into a dense large shrub or small tree, valued where few other broadleaf evergreens will tolerate constant wind and salt spray. Its thick, leathery, dark green leaves have a distinctive felted white-grey underside that shows attractively when the foliage moves in the wind, and small dark red-purple flowers in spring carry a light honey fragrance. Sticky black seeds follow in woody capsules, occasionally self-sowing near the parent plant. It takes hard pruning and shearing well, making it useful as a windbreak hedge or background screen, and establishes quickly once planted.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society)

planting.note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in summer or plant container specimens in spring in well-drained, average soil in partial shade to full sun; this variegated form grows more slowly than the plain green species and appreciates some wind shelter while young.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in partial shade to full sun; Variegated Lemonwood is a slower, more compact sport of the New Zealand lemonwood tree, prized for its glossy, wavy-margined leaves broadly edged in creamy white that brighten a shrub border or screen year-round. Crushing or bruising the foliage releases a distinct lemon scent, a signature trait of the species. In spring it produces small, sweetly honey-scented pale yellow flowers that are more noticeable by fragrance than by sight. Left unpruned it forms an upright, dense, large shrub or small tree useful as a light-reflecting focal point against darker evergreens; it also tolerates shearing for a more restrained hedge form.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in average, well-drained soil in partial to deep shade; Salicifolia is a female clone, so a male Aucuba planted nearby is needed for the bright red winter berries to form.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to deep shade; unlike most Aucuba selections grown for gold-speckled foliage, Salicifolia is prized for its plain, glossy, narrow, willow-like leaves with finely toothed margins, giving the shrub a finer, more graceful texture than the broader-leaved gold-dust forms. As a female clone it sets abundant clusters of bright red berries through winter when a male Aucuba such as 'Golden King' or 'Mr. Goldstrike' is planted within pollinating range. It shares the species' toughness in deep, dry shade under mature trees and its tolerance of urban pollution, salt spray, and heavy root competition, making it a reliable, low-maintenance backbone shrub for shaded borders.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in average, well-drained soil in partial to deep shade; Fructu Albo is a female clone and needs a male Aucuba planted nearby to set its distinctive ivory-white berries.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to deep shade; Fructu Albo offers a novel twist on a familiar shade shrub, bearing creamy white to pale ivory berries in winter instead of the typical bright red, set off nicely against its glossy, lightly gold-flecked, dark green leaves. Like other female Aucuba selections it requires a male pollinator such as 'Golden King' within range to fruit reliably. Its cultural needs match the species exactly: it thrives in deep, dry shade under established trees where few other broadleaf evergreens perform, tolerates urban pollution and salt spray, and needs only occasional light pruning to maintain a dense, rounded form.

planting.note: Plant container-grown plants in spring in humus-rich, well-drained soil in shade to partial shade; the white-margined form is slightly slower and less cold-hardy than the plain green species, so provide extra winter protection at the cold edge of its range.

directions: Plant in humus-rich, well-drained soil in shade to partial shade, sheltered from strong sun and drying wind, which can scorch the pale leaf margins. This variegated sport of the Fatsia-ivy hybrid carries the same bold, glossy, lobed foliage as the species but each leaf is irregularly edged in silvery white, brightening dim corners and pairing well with dark-leaved shade companions. Left unstaked it sprawls loosely and can be trained onto a support for a more upright accent, or tied in as an informal groundcover under high shade. It is somewhat less vigorous and less cold-tolerant than the green-leaved species, so a sheltered spot and a winter mulch are worthwhile in the coldest part of its range.

common_name: Annemieke Fatshedera (Lemon and Lime Gold-Centered Tree Ivy)

planting.note: Plant container-grown plants in spring in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Annemieke colors best with some bright, indirect light and can fade to plain green in very deep shade.

directions: Plant in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade with some bright, filtered light to keep its variegation vivid; Annemieke, also sold as 'Lemon and Lime', is a striking sport of the Fatsia-ivy hybrid with a bold splash of chartreuse to golden-yellow filling the center of each large, leathery, palmately lobed leaf. Its loose, semi-vining habit is identical to the species, sprawling gracefully or climbing a support if tied in, and small globose clusters of white flowers appear on mature growth in autumn. It needs a bit more light than the plain green form to hold its gold center, but still scorches in hot direct sun, so a bright shaded spot under high tree canopy or on a north- or east-facing wall suits it best.

common_name: John Redmond Butcher's Broom (Self-Fruiting Hermaphrodite Ruscus)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown specimens in moist to dry, well-drained soil in partial to full shade in spring; John Redmond is a hermaphrodite clone that sets its ornamental red berries on its own, without needing a separate male plant nearby.

directions: Plant divisions or container specimens in moist to dry, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; John Redmond is a compact, dense, hermaphrodite selection of butcher's broom bred to carry both male and female flower parts on every plant, so it reliably produces its glossy bright-red winter berries without needing a separate pollinator planted alongside it, unlike the straight species. This makes it a far more practical choice for small gardens, containers, and mixed plantings where space for a second Ruscus isn't available. In every other respect it shares the species' remarkable tolerance for deep, dry shade under mature trees, drought, and neglect, producing stiff, spine-tipped, dark green cladodes that stay attractive through the harshest winter conditions.
